title: One-letter extension of a reduced subword under strong exchange
statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbf R}(V)$ be a subgroup of the group of invertible real linear maps, and let $S\subseteq G\setminus\{1\}$ be a set such that $s^2=1$ for every $s\in S$ and every element of $G$ is a finite product of elements of $S$. Let $\ell(g)$ be the least number of letters in such a product, and call a word reduced when its number of letters equals the length of its product. Put $T=\{h^{-1}sh:h\in G,\ s\in S\}$. Assume the following right strong exchange property, including possibly nonreduced words: for every $n\geq0$, $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in S$ and $t\in T$, if $g=a_1\cdots a_n$ and $\ell(gt)\leq\ell(g)$, then $n\geq1$ and there is $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with
$$gt=a_1\cdots a_{j-1}a_{j+1}\cdots a_n.$$
For $q\geq0$ let $b_1,\ldots,b_q\in S$ and let $b_1\cdots b_q$ be a reduced word with product $v$. Suppose $u\in G$, $u\ne v$, and some subsequence of this word, in its original order, is a reduced word with product $u$. Then there exist a subset $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}$ and an index $r\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\setminus I$ such that the word formed by the letters at the positions in $I$, in increasing order, is reduced with product $u$, and the word formed by the positions in $I\cup\{r\}$, in increasing order, is also reduced. In particular their lengths are $\ell(u)$ and $\ell(u)+1$, respectively. Empty words are allowed; when $S=\varnothing$ or $q=0$ the hypotheses $u\ne v$ and reduced-subword containment cannot hold simultaneously.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1 and its proof, printed pp.33--34 (PDF pp.41--42, zero-based). This statement extracts the one-position insertion conclusion of that proof and replaces the Coxeter-system hypothesis by the explicit right strong exchange property it uses. Local PDF WANTED; university-hosted text read online. The delivered formulation is for a real linear subgroup, exactly the kind of group used by the parent item; no property beyond its displayed group and exchange assumptions is needed.

proof.text: Put $m=\ell(u)$ and $[q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}$. The family $\mathcal F$ of subsets $J\subseteq[q]$ whose selected word is reduced with product $u$ is finite and nonempty by hypothesis. Every $J\in\mathcal F$ has $|J|=m$. No such $J$ is $[q]$, since the full product is $v\ne u$; hence $m<q$. Choose $I\in\mathcal F$ for which $r=\max([q]\setminus I)$ is as small as possible. This uses a minimum of a nonempty finite set of integers only.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed p.33 (PDF page 41, zero-based), first sentence of the proof: minimizing the last omitted position.

proof.text: All positions strictly greater than $r$ belong to $I$. Let $A$ be the product of the selected letters before $r$, let $B=b_{r+1}\cdots b_q$, and let $P=b_1\cdots b_{r-1}$, with empty products equal to $1$. Then $u=AB$ and $v=P b_rB$. Set $t=B^{-1}b_rB\in T$ and $z=A b_rB=ut$. The word at $I\cup\{r\}$ represents $z$ and has $m+1$ letters, so $\ell(z)\le m+1$. These identities follow by cancellation; also $t^2=1$ because $b_r^2=1$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed p.33, definition of the conjugate reflection and the inserted expression; group identities written explicitly.

proof.text: Suppose this inserted word is not reduced. Its $m+1$ letters then give $\ell(z)<m+1$, hence $\ell(ut)\le m=\ell(u)$. Apply the assumed right strong exchange property to the selected word at $I$, of length $m$, and to $t$. It gives $m\ge1$ and deletion of one selected position $p\in I$ yielding $z$. Thus $p\ne r$ and either $p>r$ or $p<r$. If $m=0$, the asserted $m\ge1$ is already a contradiction, so that case needs no deletion index.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed p.33, strong-exchange application. Here the displayed non-strict exchange hypothesis applies directly; no Coxeter length-parity theorem is used.

proof.text: If $p>r$, write $B=C b_pD$, where $C=b_{r+1}\cdots b_{p-1}$ and $D=b_{p+1}\cdots b_q$. The deletion equality is $A b_rB=A C D$. Left cancellation gives $b_rB=CD$, so $v=P b_rB=P C D$. The displayed word $P C D$ is the original full word with precisely positions $r$ and $p$ removed, and has $q-2$ letters. Hence $\ell(v)\le q-2<q$, contradicting the assumed reducedness of $b_1\cdots b_q$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed pp.33--34, equation (2.8) and its contradiction: deletion in the final full suffix.

proof.text: If $p<r$, let $A_p$ be the product of the selected letters before $r$ except the letter at $p$. The deletion equality is $A b_rB=A_pB$. Right cancellation and $b_r^2=1$ give $A b_r=A_p$ and $A=A_p b_r$, hence $u=A_p b_rB$. Thus $I'=(I\setminus\{p\})\cup\{r\}$ selects another word for $u$ with exactly $m$ letters; it is reduced since $m=\ell(u)$. Its omitted set is $([q]\setminus(I\cup\{r\}))\cup\{p\}$. This is nonempty (it contains $p$), and each of its positions is less than $r$. Therefore $\max([q]\setminus I')<r$, contradicting the choice of $I$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed p.34, equation (2.9) and the minimality contradiction; includes deletions before the first originally omitted position, as in the source remark.

proof.text: Both possible deletions are impossible, so the inserted word is reduced. The original selected word at $I$ is reduced with product $u$ by its choice in $\mathcal F$, $r\notin I$, and $|I\cup\{r\}|=|I|+1=m+1$. These are all the asserted conclusions. If $q=0$, the only subword is the full empty word, giving $u=v=1$ and contradicting the hypotheses. If $S=\varnothing$, generation forces $G=\{1\}$ and the only possible word has $q=0$. Empty selected words with $q>0$ were covered by the $m=0$ contradiction in step 3.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1, printed pp.33--34, conclusion; empty-word and empty-generator cases checked explicitly.
